title: How Many Numbers in a Range Are at Most x?

concept.title: Sort the questions by x and insert the numbers in increasing order, so the tree only ever holds numbers that are small enough
body: A list is fixed and every question brings its own bound: **how many numbers at the positions `l..r` are at most `x`?** The bound changes from question to question, so a single prefix-count array cannot answer them all. For the list `4 1 7 3 5` the positions 2 to 4 hold `1 7 3`, and two of them are at most 3.

The questions do not have to be answered in the order they come, because all of them are known in advance. This is the **offline** idea: sort the questions by `x` and the positions by their value. Then sweep with a pointer: before a question with the bound `x`, insert into a Fenwick tree (indexed by position) every element whose value is at most `x` and has not been inserted yet. After that the tree holds exactly the small enough elements, so the answer is a range sum `sum(r) - sum(l - 1)`.

body.code:
order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: a[i])
p = 0
for j in sorted(range(q), key=lambda j: qs[j][2]):
    l, r, x = qs[j]
    while p < n and a[order[p]] <= x:
        bit_add(t, order[p] + 1, 1)        # this element is now "small enough"
        p += 1
    ans[j] = bit_sum(t, r) - bit_sum(t, l - 1)

body: The pointer only moves forward, so every element is inserted once, and each question costs two prefix sums. Together the work is O((n + q) log n). Offline processing in the order of a hidden parameter is one of the most useful patterns with a Fenwick tree.

statement: A list of `n` numbers is given. Answer `q` questions. Each question has three numbers `l`, `r` and `x`: count the positions between `l` and `r` (both included, counting from 1) that hold a number which is at most `x`. Print the answers on one line, in the order of the questions.
inputFormat: The first line has `n` and `q`: the length of the list and the number of questions.
The second line has the `n` numbers of the list.
Each of the next `q` lines has three numbers `l`, `r` and `x`.

examples.note: In the whole list 4, 1 and 3 are at most 4. In the positions 2..4 (1 7 3) the numbers 1 and 3 are at most 3. The position 3 holds 7, which is more than 6: 3 2 0.

hints: A single array of prefix counts does not work, because x is different in every question.
Answer the questions in the order of x, and insert the numbers into a Fenwick tree (by position) in the order of their value.
When the tree holds exactly the numbers that are at most x, the answer is sum(r) - sum(l - 1).

explanation: The questions are answered in the order of x. The numbers are inserted into a Fenwick tree over positions in the order of their value, so before each question the tree holds exactly the numbers that are at most x, and a range sum gives the answer.
solution.complexity: Time O((n + q) log n), space O(n + q).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

def bit_add(t, i, x):
    n = len(t) - 1
    while i <= n:
        t[i] += x
        i += i & -i

def bit_sum(t, i):
    s = 0
    while i > 0:
        s += t[i]
        i -= i & -i
    return s

n, q = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
qs = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(q)]

order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: a[i])
t = [0] * (n + 1)
ans = [0] * q
p = 0
for j in sorted(range(q), key=lambda j: qs[j][2]):
    l, r, x = qs[j]
    while p < n and a[order[p]] <= x:
        bit_add(t, order[p] + 1, 1)
        p += 1
    ans[j] = bit_sum(t, r) - bit_sum(t, l - 1)
print(*ans)
